children.title: Group Weighting Normalization System
children.top_down_role: Group-size, design-scale, and covariance-aware penalty choices.

children.title: Group-Size Weights
children.top_down_role: Penalty adjustments intended to account for unequal group cardinalities.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_g=\sqrt{d_g}\) and \(\Omega(\beta)=\sum_{g=1}^m\sqrt{d_g}\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2\).

notation.meaning: number of coordinates in group g

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square-root group-size convention for comparably scaled coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the group-size weighting convention, the weight of group \(G_g\) is \(w_g:=\sqrt{d_g}\), where \(d_g=|G_g|\). The resulting penalty is \[\Omega(\beta)=\sum_{g=1}^m\sqrt{d_g}\,\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2.\] This convention compensates for the typical \(\sqrt{d_g}\) growth of a Euclidean noise vector when coordinates have comparable scale; it does not itself correct unequal design scales or within-group covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning weight equal to the square root of group size compensates for the typical Euclidean magnitude of an equally scaled noise block.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Size Weights

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record clearly states the square-root group-size weighting convention, and the definition kind is suitable for this terminal container. The noise-scaling motivation depends on additional comparability or distributional assumptions and requires a precise group-Lasso normalization source.

children.title: Design-Scale Normalization
children.top_down_role: Group-level scaling based on predictor magnitude or block geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(X_g\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_g}\) is the design block for group \(G_g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_g=\|X_g\|_{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n\) and \(\|X_g/w_g\|_{\mathrm F}=\sqrt n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frobenius-scale normalization of nonzero design blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(w_g:=\|X_g\|_{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n\) and \(\widetilde X_g:=X_g/w_g\). Then \(\|\widetilde X_g\|_{\mathrm F}=\sqrt n\), and the parameterization \(X_g\beta_{G_g}=\widetilde X_g\theta_{G_g}\) with \(\theta_{G_g}=w_g\beta_{G_g}\) transforms the unweighted penalty \(\sum_g\|\theta_{G_g}\|_2\) into \[\sum_g w_g\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2.\] Thus block standardization and design-scale weighting are equivalent parameterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling each design block to common Frobenius norm is equivalent to weighting its coefficient block by the original design scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Design-Scale Normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Frobenius normalization and reparameterization are algebraically consistent, and the representation kind fits the terminal container. No source with a specific locator is supplied to establish this as a recognized design-scale normalization convention in the group-Lasso setting.

children.title: Covariance-Aware Weights
children.top_down_role: Penalty choices incorporating within-group covariance structure.

assumptions_latex: \(z_g\in\mathbb{R}^{d_g}\) is a centered score vector with covariance \(\Sigma_g\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_g=q_{1-\delta_g}(\|z_g\|_2)\), so \(\mathbb P(\|z_g\|_2\leq w_g)\geq1-\delta_g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile calibration of weights to blockwise dual-score covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A covariance-aware weight at tail level \(\delta_g\) is \[w_g:=q_{1-\delta_g}(\|z_g\|_2),\] where \(q_{1-\delta_g}\) is the upper quantile under the distribution determined by \(\Sigma_g\). It satisfies \(\mathbb P(\|z_g\|_2\leq w_g)\geq1-\delta_g\). If \(\sum_g\delta_g\leq\delta\), then \(\mathbb P(\|z_g\|_2\leq w_g\text{ for all }g)\geq1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covariance-aware weights are upper quantiles of blockwise dual-score norms, yielding simultaneous stochastic control when the allocated tail probabilities sum to the desired error level.
knowledge_statements.title: Covariance-Aware Weights

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is plausible for stochastic weight calibration, and the union-bound conclusion follows once valid marginal quantiles are defined. However, covariance Sigma_g alone does not determine the distribution or the quantile of ||z_g||_2. The record must specify the full score distribution, such as a Gaussian law, or define the quantile under an otherwise explicitly given law, and it needs an authoritative calibration source with a precise locator.

children.title: Weight Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Selection and shrinkage distortions caused by unsuitable group weights.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\beta_{G_g}=0\) if and only if \(\|X_g^\top y/n\|_2\leq\lambda w_g\); misspecified \(w_g\) therefore changes the block-selection boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact selection distortion under an orthonormal block design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an orthonormal block design, the group-Lasso solution is block soft-thresholding: \[\widehat\beta_{G_g}=\left(1-\frac{\lambda w_g}{\|u_g\|_2}\right)_+u_g,\qquad u_g:=X_g^\top y/n.\] Hence group \(g\) is excluded exactly when \(\|u_g\|_2\leq\lambda w_g\). An oversized weight can suppress a genuine block, while an undersized weight lowers its noise-entry threshold; arbitrary weights destroy scale comparability across groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under orthonormal blocks, each weight directly sets that block's selection threshold. Oversized weights cause false exclusions, while undersized weights permit noise blocks to enter.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the weight-misspecification container. Under the stated block-orthonormal least-squares assumptions, the block soft-thresholding formula and exclusion threshold are plausible, but no group-thresholding source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Group-Lasso Constraint Forms
children.top_down_role: Block-norm budget formulations and their conic interfaces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min L(\beta)\) subject to \(\Omega_w(\beta)\leq\tau\) is represented by \(\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2\leq t_g\) and \(\sum_gw_gt_g\leq\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget form and second-order-cone epigraph for disjoint groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constrained group-Lasso problem is \[\min_{\beta}L(\beta)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\Omega_w(\beta)\leq\tau.\] It has the second-order-cone representation \[\min_{\beta,t}L(\beta)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2\leq t_g\ \text{for every }g,\qquad\sum_gw_gt_g\leq\tau.\] Any penalized solution at \(\lambda\geq0\) solves the budget problem with \(\tau=\Omega_w(\widehat\beta)\); under constraint qualification, a budget solution has a nonnegative multiplier \(\lambda\) giving the penalized form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A group-norm budget becomes second-order-cone constraints using one epigraph variable per block, and its Lagrange multiplier produces the penalized formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Lasso Constraint Forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the constraint-forms container, and the block-norm budget constraints admit the displayed second-order-cone epigraph. With an arbitrary proper closed convex loss, however, only the group-norm constraints are necessarily SOC-representable; the entire optimization problem is an SOCP only when the loss epigraph also has an appropriate conic representation. The multiplier correspondence and constraint-qualification statement also require a precise source locator.

children.title: Group-Sparsity KKT Certificate Family
children.top_down_role: Active- and inactive-block optimality certificate organization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\beta\) is optimal if and only if each active block satisfies \(\nabla_gL(\widehat\beta)=-\lambda w_g\widehat\beta_{G_g}/\|\widehat\beta_{G_g}\|_2\) and each inactive block satisfies \(\|\nabla_gL(\widehat\beta)\|_2\leq\lambda w_g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient blockwise KKT certificate for differentiable convex loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(\widehat eta\) minimizes \(L( eta)+\lambda\sum_gw_g\| eta_{G_g}\|_2\) if and only if, for every \(g\), \[\widehat eta_{G_g}
eq0\ \Longrightarrow\ 
abla_gL(\widehat eta)+\lambda w_g rac{\widehat eta_{G_g}}{\|\widehat eta_{G_g}\|_2}=0,\] and \[\widehat eta_{G_g}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \|
abla_gL(\widehat eta)\|_2\leq\lambda w_g.\] These equalities and inequalities form a directly checkable active- and inactive-block optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimality is certified by exact gradient balance on nonzero blocks and a dual-norm inequality on zero blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Sparsity KKT Certificate Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind exactly fits the KKT-certificate terminal container, and the active- and inactive-block conditions are the expected subgradient optimality conditions for differentiable convex loss and positive group weights. No authoritative group-Lasso or convex-analysis source with a specific section, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Shared-Support Group Lasso Family
children.top_down_role: Shared-support formulations across responses or related tasks.

children.title: Multitask Group Lasso
children.top_down_role: Grouped regularization across related learning tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Multitask Group Lasso
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Task-specific designs with rowwise coupling of feature coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For tasks \(t=1,\ldots,T\), let \(X_t\in\mathbb{R}^{n_t\times p}\), \(y_t\in\mathbb{R}^{n_t}\), and collect task coefficients as \(B=[b_1,\ldots,b_T]\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times T}\). The multitask group-lasso estimator is any solution of
\[
\widehat B\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times T}}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{1}{2n_t}\lVert y_t-X_tb_t\rVert_2^2+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\lVert B_{j,:}\rVert_2\right\},
\]
where \(\lambda\geq0\). The row penalty permits task-dependent magnitudes while encouraging entire feature rows to vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multitask group lasso fits task-specific regressions while penalizing each feature's coefficient vector across tasks, encouraging a shared set of selected features.
assumptions_latex: \(T,p,n_t\in\mathbb{N}\) and the tasks share the same feature indexing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat B\) minimizes the joint empirical loss plus the rowwise \(\ell_{2,1}\) penalty.

notation.meaning: Row of coefficients for feature j across all tasks.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convex multitask group-lasso formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation, notation, content kind, and local scope are mathematically appropriate, but no inspectable authoritative citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Multiresponse Group Lasso
children.top_down_role: Grouped regularization across multiple response coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiresponse Group Lasso
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common design matrix and matrix-valued response with row-group regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\) and \(Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\). For a convex loss \(L:\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), the multiresponse group-lasso estimator is
\[
\widehat B\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}}\left\{L(Y,XB)+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\lVert B_{j,:}\rVert_2\right\},
\]
where \(\lambda\geq0\) and \(w_j>0\). For squared error one may take \(L(Y,XB)=\lVert Y-XB\rVert_F^2/(2n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiresponse group lasso uses one design matrix and penalizes each predictor's coefficients jointly across response coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(L(Y,\cdot)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat B\) is a convexly regularized coefficient matrix with rowwise response coupling.

notation.meaning: Coefficients of predictor j for all responses.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-design multiresponse formulation is coherent and correctly distinguished from the multitask formulation, but it lacks a cited authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Shared-Support Coupling
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms favoring common selected predictors across tasks or responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Support Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Meaning and limitation of rowwise coupling across tasks or responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times T}\), define \(\Omega(B)=\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\lVert B_{j,:}\rVert_2\) with \(w_j>0\). Its active-row set is
\[
S(B)=\{j:\lVert B_{j,:}\rVert_2>0\}=\bigcup_{t=1}^T\{j:B_{jt}\neq0\}.
\]
Thus the penalty couples the decision that feature \(j\) is absent from every task: deleting a row requires \(B_{jt}=0\) for all \(t\). It does not require equal coefficients or require \(B_{jt}\neq0\) in every task whenever row \(j\) is active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rowwise group regularization couples global feature exclusion, but an active row may still contain task-specific zeros and unequal coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(B)=\bigcup_{t=1}^T\operatorname{supp}(b_t)\), without requiring identical taskwise supports.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequence of the rowwise group norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The active-row identity and limitation of rowwise coupling are correct and fit the property container, but no inspectable citation is provided.

children.title: Task-Heterogeneity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where shared-support assumptions conflict with task-specific structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Task-Heterogeneity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representational boundary when task supports are substantially different.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(T=p=2\) and
\[
B=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad a,b\neq0.
\]
The taskwise supports are disjoint, yet the shared-row active set is \(S(B)=\{1,2\}\). Moreover, for unit weights,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^2\lVert B_{j,:}\rVert_2=|a|+|b|=\sum_{t=1}^2\lVert b_t\rVert_1.
\]
Hence rowwise multitask coupling supplies no group-penalty reduction for this disjoint-support pattern. Shared-support regularization is therefore least structurally matched when informative features vary almost entirely across tasks; it neither represents separate support budgets nor guarantees transfer benefits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With disjoint task supports, the row penalty reduces to separate coordinate penalties and provides no shared-support economy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the displayed disjoint-support family, \(\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}=\lVert b_1\rVert_1+\lVert b_2\rVert_1\).

notation.meaning: Sum of Euclidean norms of the rows of B.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed counterexample and norm identity correctly describe a task-heterogeneity boundary, but the failure-boundary interpretation has no supporting source or locator.

children.title: Sparse-Group Lasso Template
children.top_down_role: Joint group-level and within-group selection formulations.

children.title: Sparse-Group Penalty System
children.top_down_role: Two-component parameterization of coordinate and group sparsity.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Group Penalty System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-parameter convex penalty for coordinate and block sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal G\) be a partition of \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\), with weights \(w_g>0\). For \(\alpha,\beta\geq0\), define the sparse-group penalty on \(x\in\mathbb{R}^p\) by
\[
\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\alpha\lVert x\rVert_1+\beta\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_2.
\]
A sparse-group regularized estimator minimizes \(F(x)+\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\) for a proper convex loss \(F\). The coordinate term can remove entries within an active group, while the group term can remove an entire block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sparse-group system combines an l1 penalty with weighted block Euclidean penalties, controlling within-group and whole-group sparsity separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}\) is convex and is a norm whenever \(\alpha+\beta>0\).

notation.meaning: Restriction of x to coordinates in group g.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-component penalty and its norm claim are correct for a weighted partition, and definition is the proper content kind, but authoritative source support is absent.

children.title: Two-Level Sparsity Geometry
children.top_down_role: Interaction between block activation and within-block coordinate selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Level Sparsity Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential geometry separating coordinate and group activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\alpha\lVert x\rVert_1+\beta\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_2\), its block subdifferential satisfies
\[
\partial_g\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\alpha\,\partial\lVert x_g\rVert_1+\begin{cases}\{\beta w_g x_g/\lVert x_g\rVert_2\},&x_g\neq0,\\ \beta w_g\mathbb B_2^{|g|},&x_g=0.\end{cases}
\]
At a zero block, the Minkowski sum of a coordinatewise cube and a Euclidean ball determines block exclusion. At a nonzero block, the \(\ell_1\) subgradient can still support zero coordinates inside that block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient combines a coordinatewise cube with a blockwise Euclidean ball, yielding separate within-block and whole-block sparsity thresholds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subdifferential has distinct coordinate and block components at every group.

notation.meaning: Closed Euclidean unit ball in the group space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subdifferential sum rule for finite convex norms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block subdifferential formula is correct for partitioned groups and expresses the intended two-level geometry, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Sparse-Group Limiting Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coordinate-only, group-only, and mixed regions of the parameter system.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Group Limiting Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-only, group-only, and genuinely mixed parameter regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\alpha\lVert x\rVert_1+\beta\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_2,
\]
the boundary regimes are exact: if \(\beta=0\) and \(\alpha>0\), then \(\Omega_{\alpha,0}(x)=\alpha\lVert x\rVert_1\); if \(\alpha=0\) and \(\beta>0\), then \(\Omega_{0,\beta}(x)=\beta\sum_gw_g\lVert x_g\rVert_2\); and if \(\alpha=\beta=0\), no regularization remains. The interior regime \(\alpha>0\), \(\beta>0\) simultaneously penalizes coordinate and group activity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Setting either parameter to zero recovers lasso or group lasso; positive values for both give the mixed sparse-group regime.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a weighted partition with \(w_g>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameter quadrant separates coordinate-only, group-only, unregularized, and mixed regimes exactly.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate specialization of the sparse-group penalty

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limiting regimes follow exactly from the stated penalty and fit the property container, but the record contains no inspectable citation.

children.title: Sparse-Group Proximal Representation
children.top_down_role: Nested coordinate and block structure used by composite solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Group Proximal Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form nested shrinkage for nonoverlapping sparse-group blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal G\) partition \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\), and let \(S_\tau\) denote coordinatewise soft thresholding, \((S_\tau(z))_i=\operatorname{sign}(z_i)(|z_i|-\tau)_+\). For \(\gamma,\alpha,\beta\geq0\), the proximal map of the sparse-group penalty is blockwise
\[
\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}}(z)\bigr)_g=\left(1-\frac{\gamma\beta w_g}{\lVert S_{\gamma\alpha}(z_g)\rVert_2}\right)_+S_{\gamma\alpha}(z_g),
\]
with the expression defined as zero when \(S_{\gamma\alpha}(z_g)=0\). Thus coordinate soft thresholding precedes block radial shrinkage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For disjoint groups, the sparse-group proximal operator applies coordinate soft thresholding and then group Euclidean shrinkage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}}\) equals nested coordinate and block shrinkage on each group.

notation.meaning: Positive part of the scalar u.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard proximal identity for a partitioned sparse-group norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested soft-thresholding and block-shrinkage representation is correct for nonoverlapping groups, but this nontrivial proximal identity requires an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Overlapping-Latent Group Family
children.top_down_role: Group systems in which coordinates participate in multiple structural units.

children.title: Direct Overlap Penalties
children.top_down_role: Penalties evaluated directly on intersecting coordinate groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Overlap Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group norms evaluated directly on possibly intersecting coordinate restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal G\) be a finite family of nonempty subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\), not necessarily disjoint, and let \(w_g>0\). The direct overlapping-group penalty is
\[
\Omega_{\mathrm{dir}}(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_2,
\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^p.
\]
A coordinate belonging to several groups enters every corresponding summand. The functional is convex and positively homogeneous; it is a norm precisely when every coordinate is covered, namely \(\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal G}g=\{1,\ldots,p\}\). Otherwise it is a seminorm whose kernel consists of vectors supported on uncovered coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct overlap penalty sums norms of the original subvectors, so coordinates in several groups are penalized repeatedly.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is finite and each \(g\in\mathcal G\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega_{\mathrm{dir}}\) is convex, and it is a norm exactly when the groups cover all coordinates.

notation.meaning: Restriction of x to group g.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard direct overlapping-group norm definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The direct overlapping-group definition and norm-versus-seminorm characterization are correct, but no relevant cited source or locator is present.

children.title: Latent Group Formulations
children.top_down_role: Variable-splitting representations that allocate effects among overlapping groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Latent Group Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal variable-splitting representation for overlapping groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a group family \(\mathcal G\) covering \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and weights \(w_g>0\), define
\[
\Omega_{\mathrm{lat}}(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}w_g\lVert v^g\rVert_2:\ x=\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}v^g,\ \operatorname{supp}(v^g)\subseteq g\right\}.
\]
Each feasible collection allocates the observed coefficient vector among group-supported latent components. The infimum is attained in finite dimensions, and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{lat}}\) is a norm. Unlike a direct overlap penalty, a coordinate shared by several groups may be assigned among them rather than necessarily charged in every group norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The latent formulation decomposes a coefficient vector into group-supported components and minimizes their weighted norm sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega_{\mathrm{lat}}\) is the minimum weighted component norm over all group-supported decompositions of \(x\).

notation.meaning: Latent component supported within group g.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard latent overlapping-group norm representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The latent variable-splitting representation is mathematically coherent, including attainment and the norm claim under coverage, but it lacks inspectable authoritative support.

children.title: Hierarchical Tree-Group Family
children.top_down_role: Nested-selection structures encoded by group systems.

children.title: Hierarchical Group Systems
children.top_down_role: Nested group systems encoding precedence among selected components.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Group Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested group families indexed by a rooted tree hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((V,\preceq)\) be a finite rooted tree order on coefficient indices, where \(u\preceq v\) means that \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\). For each \(v\in V\), define its descendant set by \(D(v)=\{u\in V:v\preceq u\}\). A descendant-based hierarchical group system consists of \(\mathcal G=\{D(v):v\in V\}\) and weights \(w_g>0\), with direct hierarchical penalty
\[
\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_2.
\]
The descendant sets are nested or disjoint. Consequently, zeroing a group removes an entire descendant region, while the overlapping nested groups couple penalization across successive hierarchy levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A descendant-based hierarchical group system assigns norms to the nested or disjoint descendant subtrees of a rooted tree, coupling coefficient removal across hierarchy levels.
assumptions_latex: \((V,\preceq)\) is a finite rooted tree order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega_{\mathcal G}\) is a convex penalty built from a laminar family of descendant groups.

notation.meaning: Descendant set rooted at node v, including v.
Ancestor order of the rooted tree.
Coefficient subvector indexed by group g.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: descendant groups of a rooted tree form a laminar hierarchical group system

children.title: Tree-Structured Groups
children.top_down_role: Group systems organized by rooted or branching inclusion structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Structured Groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laminarity condition characterizing groups compatible with a rooted tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite group family \(\mathcal G\subseteq2^{\{1,\ldots,p\}}\) is tree-structured when it is laminar:
\[
\forall g,h\in\mathcal G,\qquad g\cap h\in\{\varnothing,g,h\}.
\]
Equivalently, any two groups are disjoint or one contains the other. Ordering groups by inclusion then gives a forest; if \(\mathcal G\) contains a unique maximal group covering every coordinate, the inclusion forest is a rooted tree. Descendant sets of nodes in a rooted tree form such a laminar family, and every finite laminar family admits an inclusion-tree representation after adjoining a root when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree-structured groups are laminar: every pair is disjoint or nested, so inclusion organizes the family as a tree or forest.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a finite family of nonempty coordinate subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is tree-structured if and only if every pair of groups is disjoint or nested.

notation.meaning: Inclusion relation defining ancestry among groups.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The laminarity condition and inclusion-tree characterization are mathematically appropriate for this condition container, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Ancestral Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection patterns constrained by ancestor–descendant relationships.

knowledge_statements.title: Ancestral Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ancestral closure for active latent groups indexed by a rooted tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,E)\) be a rooted tree and let \(A(v)\subseteq V\) contain \(v\) and all its ancestors. Suppose \(\beta=\sum_{v\in V}z^{v}\), where \(\operatorname{supp}(z^{v})\subseteq A(v)\). Define the latent active set by \(I=\{v:z^{v}\ne0\}\) and the selected coordinate set by \(S=\bigcup_{v\in I}A(v)\). Then \(S\) is ancestrally closed: \(u\in S\) implies \(A(u)\subseteq S\). Thus selection expressed as a union of ancestor groups cannot include a node without also selecting every ancestor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support assembled from active ancestor groups is closed upward toward the root: selecting any node also selects all its ancestors.
assumptions_latex: Each latent vector \(z^{v}\) is supported on \(A(v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in S\Longrightarrow A(u)\subseteq S\).

notation.meaning: Node v together with all its ancestors
Latent vector associated with node v
Selected coordinate set induced by active latent groups

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is internally correct for the explicitly defined ancestor groups and fits the Ancestral Selection leaf, but no source is cited to establish that this group convention matches the intended hierarchical latent-group formulation.

children.title: Hierarchy Violations
children.top_down_role: Selection regimes conflicting with the intended nesting structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy Violations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate that a proposed support violates ancestral closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted tree \(T=(V,E)\) and proposed selected set \(S\subseteq V\), a hierarchy violation is certified by a pair \((u,v)\) such that \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\), \(v\in S\), and \(u\notin S\). Equivalently, with \(A(v)\) denoting the ancestors of \(v\), including \(v\), the support is hierarchy-compatible exactly when \(A(v)\subseteq S\) for every \(v\in S\). Hence one omitted ancestor of one selected node is a finite, directly verifiable certificate of incompatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected node paired with any unselected ancestor certifies that the proposed support violates the hierarchy.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq V\) is the proposed selected support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) violates ancestral closure if and only if \(\exists v\in S\) with \(A(v)\nsubseteq S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite certificate and its equivalent ancestral-closure condition are mathematically precise, and certificate is the appropriate content kind for this leaf. An authoritative source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Overlap Identifiability Failures
children.top_down_role: Redundant group systems and nonunique latent allocations.

children.title: Redundant Group Systems
children.top_down_role: Group collections containing duplicative or structurally unnecessary coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Group Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonidentifiability caused by interchangeable latent groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G\) index latent vectors \((v_g)_{g\in\mathcal G}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{supp}(v_g)\subseteq g\) and \(\beta=\sum_g v_g\). If distinct groups \(g_1,g_2\) have the same support and equal positive weights, then any feasible allocation with \(v_{g_1}+v_{g_2}=z\ne0\) admits the continuum \(v_{g_1}=tz\), \(v_{g_2}=(1-t)z\), where \(0\le t\le1\). Every such allocation has the same contribution \(w\lVert z\rVert_2\) to the latent group penalty. The represented coefficient \(\beta\) may therefore be identifiable while its group allocation is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate equally weighted groups can split the same vector continuously without changing either the represented coefficient or penalty value.
assumptions_latex: \(g_1=g_2\) as coordinate sets and both weights equal \(w>0\).
The latent penalty is \(\sum_g w_g\lVert v_g\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\ne0\Longrightarrow\) the latent allocation between \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) is nonunique.

notation.meaning: Latent vector supported on group g

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed aligned allocations establish nonuniqueness for duplicate equally weighted groups, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No inspectable source supports the latent-penalty convention or its interpretation as a redundant-group identifiability failure.

children.title: Latent Allocation Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Nonunique decomposition of coefficient effects across latent groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Latent Allocation Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambiguity of minimum-penalty decompositions in an overlapping latent norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal G\) be a finite family of coordinate groups with weights \(w_g>0\). For \(\beta\in\mathbb R^p\), define the optimal-allocation set
\[
\mathcal A(\beta)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{(v_g)}\left\{\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}w_g\lVert v_g\rVert_2:\ \sum_{g\in\mathcal G}v_g=\beta,\ \operatorname{supp}(v_g)\subseteq g\right\}.
\]
The representation has latent allocation ambiguity at \(\beta\) when \(\mathcal A(\beta)\) contains at least two distinct tuples. This ambiguity concerns the latent decomposition and does not by itself imply nonuniqueness of \(\beta\) in a regularized learning problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocation ambiguity occurs when one coefficient vector has multiple distinct group-supported decompositions attaining the same minimum latent penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is finite and covers every coordinate under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Latent allocation ambiguity at \(\beta\) means \(\lvert\mathcal A(\beta)\rvert>1\).

notation.meaning: Set of minimum-penalty latent allocations of beta
Latent vector supported on group g

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent definition of ambiguity in minimum-penalty latent decompositions and correctly distinguishes allocation nonuniqueness from coefficient nonuniqueness. It lacks the required authoritative citation and specific locator.

children.title: Identifiability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where group-level attribution cannot be uniquely interpreted.

knowledge_statements.title: Identifiability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniqueness condition for an optimal latent allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On the product space of group-supported latent vectors, define \(S(v)=\sum_g v_g\) and \(R(v)=\sum_g w_g\lVert v_g\rVert_2\). For an optimal allocation \(v^\star\) of \(\beta\), define the descent cone
\[
\mathcal D_R(v^\star)=\{h:\exists t>0,\ R(v^\star+th)\le R(v^\star)\}.
\]
Then \(v^\star\) is the unique minimum-penalty allocation of \(\beta\) if and only if
\[
\ker S\cap\mathcal D_R(v^\star)=\{0\}.
\]
A nonzero vector in this intersection preserves the represented coefficient while producing a distinct allocation with no larger penalty, and therefore marks the identifiability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal latent allocation is unique exactly when no nonzero coefficient-preserving perturbation lies in the penalty’s descent cone.
assumptions_latex: The group family is finite and all weights are positive.
\(v^\star\) attains the latent allocation minimum for \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^\star\text{ is unique}\Longleftrightarrow\ker S\cap\mathcal D_R(v^\star)=\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: Summation map from latent vectors to the represented coefficient
Weighted sum of latent group norms
Descent cone of R at the optimal allocation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The kernel-intersection condition is plausible for the displayed descent-direction convention and condition is an appropriate knowledge kind, but the exact descent-cone convention and uniqueness equivalence require source alignment before acceptance.

children.title: Duplicate-Group Effects
children.top_down_role: Penalty and allocation consequences of repeated group definitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Duplicate-Group Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective weight and allocation behavior of duplicated groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose two indexed latent groups have the same coordinate set and weights \(w_1,w_2>0\). For their combined contribution \(z\),
\[
\inf_{v_1+v_2=z}\bigl(w_1\lVert v_1\rVert_2+w_2\lVert v_2\rVert_2\bigr)=\min\{w_1,w_2\}\lVert z\rVert_2.
\]
If \(w_1<w_2\), every minimizer assigns \(z\) to the first copy and zero to the second. If \(w_1=w_2\) and \(z\ne0\), all aligned splits \(v_1=tz\), \(v_2=(1-t)z\), with \(0\le t\le1\), are optimal. Duplication therefore changes the effective weight only through the smallest duplicate weight but can destroy allocation uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate groups act like one group with the smallest duplicate weight; tied weights create nonunique latent splits.
assumptions_latex: The two indexed groups have identical coordinate support.
Their penalties are weighted Euclidean norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective duplicate-group weight is \(\min\{w_1,w_2\}\), with nonunique splitting when \(w_1=w_2\) and \(z\ne0\).

notation.meaning: Latent contributions assigned to the duplicate groups

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The effective-weight formula and the stated tied-weight aligned splits are mathematically consistent for weighted Euclidean latent penalties, and property fits the leaf. A source with a specific locator is absent.

children.title: Group-Sparsity Theory Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Navigation to block-adapted statistical and recovery theory without importing theorem payload.

children.title: Group-Restricted Geometry Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Navigation to block-adapted curvature, isometry, and null-space conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Restricted Geometry Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-restricted curvature condition for group-sparse estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), let \(\mathcal G\) be a partition of the coordinates, and let \(J\subseteq\mathcal G\) contain at most \(s\) groups. For \(h\in\mathbb R^p\), write \(h_J\) for its restriction to their union. A group restricted-eigenvalue condition with cone constant \(c>0\) and curvature \(\kappa>0\) holds when
\[
\frac{\lVert Xh\rVert_2}{\sqrt n}\ge\kappa\lVert h_J\rVert_2
\]
for every such \(J\) and every nonzero \(h\) satisfying \(\sum_{g\notin J}w_g\lVert h_g\rVert_2\le c\sum_{g\in J}w_g\lVert h_g\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group-restricted curvature lower-bounds prediction change on every block-sparse error cone by the error magnitude on its active groups.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a coordinate partition and \(w_g>0\).
The active group set has cardinality at most \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert Xh\rVert_2/\sqrt n\ge\kappa\lVert h_J\rVert_2\) on every specified group cone.

notation.meaning: Restriction of h to the union of groups in J

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The candidate gives a legitimate block restricted-eigenvalue condition and is suitable as a condition within this geometry-interface topic. Because normalization, weighting, and cone conventions vary, an authoritative source with an exact locator is necessary.

children.title: Group-Support Recovery Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Navigation to exact and approximate block-selection guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Support Recovery Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block irrepresentability condition used for exact active-group recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) have columns partitioned into groups, let \(S\) be the true active-group set, and assume \(X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S\) is invertible. For a group-normalized coefficient direction \(u_S\), exact group-support recovery is commonly interfaced through the strict dual-feasibility condition
\[
\max_{g\notin S}\frac{1}{w_g}\left\lVert X_g^{\mathsf T}X_S(X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S)^{-1}u_S\right\rVert_2<1.
\]
Here each active block of \(u_S\) equals \(w_h\beta_h^\star/\lVert\beta_h^\star\rVert_2\). This condition controls false group inclusion; complete recovery additionally requires signal-strength and noise bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict block dual feasibility limits inactive-group correlation with the active design; signal and noise conditions are additionally needed for exact recovery.
assumptions_latex: The true active blocks \(\beta_h^\star\) are nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every inactive block has normalized dual score strictly below \(1\).

notation.meaning: Weighted blockwise coefficient direction on active groups

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement properly presents strict block dual feasibility as an interface rather than a standalone recovery theorem, so condition fits the container. Its scaling and weighted block-direction formula are convention-dependent and unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Group-Misspecification Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Navigation to theory for incorrect partitions, overlaps, or hierarchies.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Misspecification Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irreducible approximation error from an incorrect structured-support family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathfrak M_{\mathcal G,s}\) be the union of coordinate subspaces generated by at most \(s\) admissible groups from a proposed system \(\mathcal G\). For a target \(\beta^
atural\in\mathbb R^p\) and design \(X\), define the prediction misspecification radius
\[
\delta_{\mathcal G,s}(\beta^
atural)=\inf_{b\in\mathfrak M_{\mathcal G,s}}\frac{\lVert X(b-\beta^
atural)\rVert_2}{\sqrt n}.
\]
If this radius is positive, every estimator constrained to \(\mathfrak M_{\mathcal G,s}\) has prediction error at least \(\delta_{\mathcal G,s}(\beta^
atural)\), even with noiseless observations \(y=X\beta^
atural\). Thus incorrect partitions, overlaps, or hierarchies create an irreducible structured approximation term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the true parameter lies a positive prediction distance from the proposed group model, no estimator restricted to that model can recover it exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak M_{\mathcal G,s}\) contains precisely the supports permitted by the proposed group structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\delta_{\mathcal G,s}(\beta^
atural)>0\Longrightarrow \lVert X(\widehat\beta-\beta^
atural)\rVert_2/\sqrt n\ge\delta_{\mathcal G,s}(\beta^
atural)\) for every \(\widehat\beta\in\mathfrak M_{\mathcal G,s}\).

notation.meaning: Parameters supported on at most s admissible groups

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower bound follows from the defined prediction distance and failure_boundary fits the misspecification-interface topic. The precise admissible-group model and its connection to incorrect partitions, overlaps, or hierarchies need an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Operator-Structured Penalty Family
children.top_down_role: Regularization templates defined through analysis operators, differences, graphs, or ordered structure.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: The Solution Path of the Generalized Lasso
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Generalized Lasso, fused models, duality, and path structure

children.title: Generalized Lasso Family
children.top_down_role: Sparse regularization after a linear analysis transform.

children.title: Analysis Sparsity
children.top_down_role: Sparse transformed coefficients and cosparse parameter geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Analysis Sparsity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparsity and cosparsity induced by a linear analysis operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}\) be a fixed linear analysis operator and \(\beta\in\mathbb R^p\). The vector \(\beta\) is analysis \(s\)-sparse when
\[
\lVert D\beta\rVert_0\le s.
\]
Its analysis support is \(S=\{i:(D\beta)_i\ne0\}\), its cosupport is \(\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,m\}\setminus S\), and its cosparsity is \(\lvert\Lambda\rvert=m-\lVert D\beta\rVert_0\). For a fixed cosupport \(\Lambda\), the corresponding cosparse model is the linear subspace \(\{\beta:D_\Lambda\beta=0\}=\ker D_\Lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Analysis sparsity means that applying a fixed linear operator produces few nonzeros; the zero rows define a cosupport and a corresponding nullspace model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert D\beta\rVert_0\le s\), with fixed-cosupport model \(\ker D_\Lambda\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definitions of analysis sparsity, support, cosupport, cosparsity, and the fixed-cosupport nullspace model are consistent, and definition is the correct content kind. No source reference or locator is supplied.

children.title: Analysis–Synthesis Distinction
children.top_down_role: Alternative structural representations and their generally different model classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Analysis–Synthesis Distinction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of sparse analysis coefficients with sparse dictionary representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an analysis operator \(D\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}\) and a synthesis dictionary \(\Psi\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\), define
\[
\mathcal M_{\mathrm{an}}(s)=\{\beta:\lVert D\beta\rVert_0\le s\},\qquad
\mathcal M_{\mathrm{syn}}(s)=\{\Psi\alpha:\lVert\alpha\rVert_0\le s\}.
\]
These model classes are generally different: analysis sparsity constrains transformed coefficients, whereas synthesis sparsity asserts the existence of a sparse generating vector. If \(D\) is square and invertible and \(\Psi=D^{-1}\), then \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{an}}(s)=\mathcal M_{\mathrm{syn}}(s)\). Without this invertible correspondence, equality does not hold in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Analysis models constrain a transform of the parameter; synthesis models generate the parameter from sparse coefficients. They coincide under an invertible matched transform-dictionary pair.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(\Psi\) are fixed linear maps of the displayed dimensions.
The same sparsity budget \(s\) is used for comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\text{ invertible and }\Psi=D^{-1}\Longrightarrow\mathcal M_{\mathrm{an}}(s)=\mathcal M_{\mathrm{syn}}(s)\); otherwise equality is not guaranteed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The analysis and synthesis model classes are clearly distinguished, and the matched square-invertible case is correct. Representation fits this comparison leaf, but the record has no authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Transform Nullspaces
children.top_down_role: Unpenalized directions and identifiability induced by rank-deficient analysis operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Transform Nullspaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unpenalized directions and coercivity of the generalized-lasso objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
F(\beta)=\frac12\lVert y-X\beta\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert D\beta\rVert_1,
\qquad \lambda>0.
\]
Every direction \(h\in\ker D\) is unpenalized because \(D(\beta+th)=D\beta\) for all \(t\in\mathbb R\). If additionally \(h\in\ker X\), then \(F(\beta+th)=F(\beta)\) for all \(t\), so any minimizer lies on a nonunique affine line. In finite dimensions, \(F\) is coercive exactly when \(\ker X\cap\ker D=\{0\}\). Thus the common nullspace is the basic identifiability and existence interface for rank-deficient analysis operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directions in the transform nullspace are unpenalized; directions also invisible to the design cause nonunique affine solution sets and destroy coercivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker X\cap\ker D\ne\{0\}\) yields invariant affine directions, while coercivity holds exactly when \(\ker X\cap\ker D=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Directions invisible to the data-fit term

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The invariance statements and finite-dimensional coercivity criterion are mathematically plausible, and property fits the Transform Nullspaces leaf. The final characterization as an existence interface is not established by the displayed coercivity result alone, and the entire claim lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Generalized-Lasso Dual Geometry
children.top_down_role: Dual constraints, boundary sets, and primal structural transitions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\beta=y-D^{\mathsf T}\widehat u\), with structural transitions possible when the dual boundary set changes.

notation.meaning: Dual boundary set at a dual solution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signal-approximation generalized lasso with squared loss; no design matrix is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal problem \(\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\frac12\|y-\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|D\beta\|_1\). Its dual is \[\max_{u\in\mathbb{R}^m:\,\|u\|_\infty\leq\lambda}\left\{y^{\mathsf T}D^{\mathsf T}u-\frac12\|D^{\mathsf T}u\|_2^2\right\}.\] For any dual maximizer \(\widehat u\), the primal minimizer satisfies \(\widehat\beta=y-D^{\mathsf T}\widehat u\). The set \(B(\widehat u)=\{i:|\widehat u_i|=\lambda\}\) identifies active dual-box faces. Along a regularization path, changes in this boundary set are candidate transition points for the structural pattern encoded by \(D\widehat\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized-lasso dual is a box-constrained quadratic problem. Its active box faces describe boundary coordinates and possible changes in the primal analysis pattern.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Lasso Dual Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual formulation and primal recovery relation are mathematically plausible and fit the dual-geometry container, but no citation supports the generalized-lasso dual or the boundary-set transition claim. A source with a specific theorem, section, or page is required.

children.title: Fusion Total-Variation Family
children.top_down_role: Piecewise-constant and graph-coupled regularization families.

children.title: One-Dimensional Fused Lasso
children.top_down_role: Ordered coefficient fusion with optional coordinate sparsity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The penalty promotes both zero coefficients and equality of adjacent coefficients.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity-design denoising formulation on an ordered one-dimensional index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_1\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times n}\) satisfy \((D_1\beta)_i=\beta_{i+1}-\beta_i\). The one-dimensional fused-lasso estimator is any solution of \[\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\frac12\|y-\beta\|_2^2+\lambda_1\|\beta\|_1+\lambda_2\|D_1\beta\|_1.\] The term weighted by \(\lambda_1\) permits coordinate sparsity, while the term weighted by \(\lambda_2\) penalizes jumps between consecutive coordinates. If \(\lambda_1=0\), the formulation is one-dimensional total-variation denoising.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-dimensional fused lasso combines squared-error fitting, optional coefficient sparsity, and an absolute-difference penalty that encourages adjacent coefficients to share values.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Fused Lasso

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The identity-design one-dimensional fused-lasso definition is precise and appropriately classified, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the formulation or its total-variation special case.

children.title: Graph Fused Lasso
children.top_down_role: Fusion penalties defined by graph incidence structure.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite oriented graph with \(|V|=n\), and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph penalty promotes equality of fitted values across adjacent vertices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted graph-incidence formulation with an optional coordinate-sparsity term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an orientation of each edge \(e=(i,j)\) and define \((D_G\beta)_e=w_e(\beta_i-\beta_j)\). The graph fused-lasso estimator is any solution of \[\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\frac12\|y-\beta\|_2^2+\lambda_1\|\beta\|_1+\lambda_G\|D_G\beta\|_1.\] Reversing an edge orientation changes one row sign and therefore leaves \(\|D_G\beta\|_1\) invariant. Vanishing entries of \(D_G\widehat\beta\) correspond exactly to graph edges whose endpoint estimates are fused.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph fused lasso penalizes weighted differences across graph edges, encouraging neighboring vertices to have equal fitted values; coordinate sparsity may be added separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Fused Lasso

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted graph-incidence formulation, orientation invariance, and fusion characterization are coherent and fit the container, but none is supported by a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Total-Variation Geometry Pair
children.top_down_role: Directional and coupled spatial-variation geometries.

children.title: Anisotropic Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Spatial variation organized through separately aggregated directional components.

assumptions_latex: \(x=(x_{i,j})\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times c}\), with forward differences taken only where the neighboring pixel exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)\) sums horizontal and vertical variation separately.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete two-dimensional forward-difference convention with omitted out-of-domain differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the discrete anisotropic total variation by \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{c-1}|x_{i,j+1}-x_{i,j}|+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}\sum_{j=1}^{c}|x_{i+1,j}-x_{i,j}|.\] Equivalently, it is the entrywise \(\ell_1\) norm of the stacked horizontal and vertical forward differences. Because the two directional differences are charged separately, the local contribution at an interior pixel is \(|(\nabla_hx)_{i,j}|+|(\nabla_vx)_{i,j}|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic total variation adds the absolute horizontal and vertical differences separately at each valid grid location.
knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic Total Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula correctly defines anisotropic TV under the stated forward-difference convention, but the convention and equivalence claim have no cited source.

children.title: Isotropic Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Spatial variation organized through locally coupled directional components.

assumptions_latex: \(x=(x_{i,j})\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times c}\), and missing forward differences at the boundary are set to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\) couples the two directional differences through a local Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete two-dimensional forward-gradient convention with zero boundary differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \((
abla_hx)_{i,j}=x_{i,j+1}-x_{i,j}\) when \(j<c\) and zero otherwise, and set \((
abla_vx)_{i,j}=x_{i+1,j}-x_{i,j}\) when \(i<r\) and zero otherwise. The discrete isotropic total variation is \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{c}\sqrt{(
abla_hx)_{i,j}^2+(
abla_vx)_{i,j}^2}.\] Thus each pixel contributes the Euclidean magnitude of its two-component forward gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isotropic total variation takes the Euclidean magnitude of the horizontal and vertical differences together, then sums those magnitudes over pixels.
knowledge_statements.title: Isotropic Total Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The isotropic-TV definition is internally consistent with zero boundary differences and fits the leaf, but the discretization and boundary convention lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Directional-Coupling Contrast
children.top_down_role: Geometric and modeling differences between separated and coupled directional variation.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times c}\), using the same discrete forward differences for both functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\leq\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)\leq\sqrt2\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise norm comparison under a common grid and boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each grid location, the anisotropic contribution is \(|a_{i,j}|+|b_{i,j}|\), whereas the isotropic contribution is \(\sqrt{a_{i,j}^2+b_{i,j}^2}\). The norm inequalities on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) give \[\sqrt{a_{i,j}^2+b_{i,j}^2}\leq |a_{i,j}|+|b_{i,j}|\leq\sqrt2\sqrt{a_{i,j}^2+b_{i,j}^2}.\] Summing yields \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\leq\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)\leq\sqrt2\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x).\] Isotropic total variation couples directions locally; anisotropic total variation remains separable by direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isotropic TV couples horizontal and vertical changes, while anisotropic TV adds them separately; their values differ by at most a factor of square root two.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional-Coupling Contrast

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm comparison and directional-coupling contrast are mathematically correct under a common grid convention and appropriately classified as a property, but the record contains no evidence reference or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Fusion Level-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Segment, region, and graph-component organization induced by fusion.

children.title: Segment Fusion
children.top_down_role: Formation of constant segments over ordered domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Segment Fusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial definition for an ordered coefficient vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A fused segment of \( eta\) is a nonempty interval \(S=[a,b]_{\mathbb Z}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \( eta_a= eta_{a+1}=\cdots= eta_b\). It is maximal when \(a=1\) or \( eta_{a-1}
eq eta_a\), and \(b=n\) or \( eta_b
eq eta_{b+1}\). The maximal fused segments are pairwise disjoint, cover every index, and are precisely the connected components of the path graph after removing edges \((i,i+1)\) for which \( eta_{i+1}- eta_i
eq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fused segment is a contiguous run of equal coefficients. Maximal runs partition the ordered indices, with nonzero adjacent differences separating neighboring segments.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is indexed in its natural order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximal fused segments form a unique partition of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

children.title: Spatial Level Sets
children.top_down_role: Region structure induced by spatial total-variation regularization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The spatial level sets are the connected components of equal-valued induced subgraphs.

notation.meaning: Subgraph induced by a vertex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based level sets requiring both equal value and spatial connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each attained value \(c\in\beta(V)\), define the ordinary level set \(L_c=\{v\in V:\beta_v=c\}\). A spatial level set is a vertex set \(S\subseteq V\) that is a connected component of the induced subgraph \(G[L_c]\) for some \(c\). Consequently, \(\beta\) is constant on \(S\), every two vertices of \(S\) are joined by an equal-valued path within \(S\), and no strictly larger vertex set has both properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spatial level set is a maximal connected region of graph vertices on which the fitted signal has one common value.
knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Level Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and matches the spatial-level-set leaf, but the convention that spatial level sets are connected components of equal-valued induced subgraphs requires a cited source.

children.title: Graph Components
children.top_down_role: Fused parameter regions organized by graph connectivity.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, \(D_G\) is an oriented incidence matrix, and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The connected components of \((V,E_0(\beta))\) are exactly the maximal connected constant regions of \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connected-component characterization induced by zero graph differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(E_0(\beta)=\{e\in E:(D_G\beta)_e=0\}\). Along every edge of \(E_0(\beta)\), the endpoint values coincide, so \(\beta\) is constant on each connected component of \(G_0(\beta)=(V,E_0(\beta))\). Conversely, any connected vertex set on which \(\beta\) is constant uses only edges in \(E_0(\beta)\) and is contained in one component of \(G_0(\beta)\). Hence these components are precisely the maximal connected constant regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keeping only graph edges whose endpoint estimates agree splits the graph into components, and those components are exactly the maximal connected constant regions.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-difference component characterization is correct for an incidence operator and fits the graph-components leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Fusion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Interfaces separating fused segments, regions, or graph components.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, \(D_G\) is an oriented incidence matrix, and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fusion boundaries are exactly the edges supporting the nonzero vector \(D_G\beta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge boundary of graph-fused constant regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fusion boundary of \(\beta\) is \[\partial_G\beta=\{e=(i,j)\in E:\beta_i\neq\beta_j\}=\operatorname{supp}(D_G\beta).\] Removing \(\partial_G\beta\) from \(G\) leaves the fused-edge subgraph, whose connected components are constant regions of \(\beta\). Every boundary edge joins vertices with different fitted values and therefore cannot lie within one such component. The definition is independent of the arbitrary orientation used to construct \(D_G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fusion boundaries are graph edges across which the fitted value changes. Removing them leaves the connected constant regions of the fitted signal.
knowledge_statements.title: Fusion Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary set is consistently identified with incidence-vector support and is orientation independent, but the fusion-boundary terminology and characterization lack cited evidence.

children.title: Trend Filtering Family
children.top_down_role: Higher-order discrete-variation regularization for locally adaptive trends.

children.title: Univariate Trend Filtering
children.top_down_role: Ordered higher-order difference regularization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimator penalizes discrete differences of order \(k+1\), promoting a piecewise degree-\(k\) sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equally spaced univariate observations with the standard discrete-difference parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times n}\) be the first forward-difference matrix and recursively let \(D^{(r)}=D_{n-r}D^{(r-1)}\), where \(D_q\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times(q+1)}\) is a first-difference matrix. The order-\(k\) univariate trend-filtering estimate is any solution of \[\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\frac12\|y-\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|D^{(k+1)}\beta\|_1.\] Its knots are the indices corresponding to nonzero entries of \(D^{(k+1)}\widehat\beta\); between knots, the \((k+1)\)-st differences vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order-k trend filtering fits an ordered signal while sparsifying its differences of order k+1, producing discrete piecewise-polynomial behavior with data-adaptive knots.
knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Trend Filtering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization template and recursive difference dimensions are coherent, but the order convention, knot indexing, and discrete piecewise-polynomial interpretation require an authoritative citation with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Univariate trend-filtering formulation and piecewise-polynomial structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the order-k equally spaced formulation, its stated structural properties, and the irregular-grid linear formulation. The underspecified minimax-rate attribution is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), \(N\ge k+2\), \(y\in\mathbb R^N\), and \(\lambda\ge 0\), order-\(k\) trend filtering solves
\[\widehat\theta\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R^N}\left\{\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\theta_i)^2+\lambda\lVert D^{(k+1)}\theta\rVert_1\right\},\]
where \(D^{(k+1)}\in\mathbb R^{(N-k-1)\times N}\) computes discrete differences of order \(k+1\). The resulting fit is piecewise polynomial of degree \(k\), with knots selected by the optimization; if it has \(m\) knots, its stated estimated degrees of freedom are \(m+k+1\). For distinct ordered positions \(x_1<\cdots<x_N\), the irregular-grid linear variant solves
\[\widehat\theta\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R^N}\left\{\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\theta_i)^2+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}\left|\frac{\theta_{i+2}-\theta_{i+1}}{x_{i+2}-x_{i+1}}-\frac{\theta_{i+1}-\theta_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i}\right|\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order-k trend filtering penalizes absolute discrete differences of order k+1 and produces an adaptively knotted piecewise-polynomial fit of degree k. A fit with m knots has stated estimated degrees of freedom m+k+1. For unequally spaced ordered inputs, linear trend filtering penalizes changes between adjacent empirical slopes.
assumptions_latex: D^{(k+1)}\in\mathbb R^{(N-k-1)\times N}\text{ computes differences of order }k+1
x_1<\cdots<x_N\text{ for the irregular-grid linear variant}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\theta\text{ is piecewise polynomial of degree }k,\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{df}}=m+k+1\text{ when the fit has }m\text{ knots, with the stated slope-difference penalty for irregular-grid linear trend filtering.}

children.title: Graph Trend Filtering
children.top_down_role: Higher-order graph-difference regularization.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite oriented graph with incidence matrix \(D\), \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}\), \(k\geq0\), and \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimator sparsifies the order-\((k+1)\) graph-difference vector \(\Delta_G^{(k+1)}\beta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph trend filtering under the alternating incidence and transpose recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\Delta_G^{(1)}=D\). For \(r\geq1\), define \(\Delta_G^{(r+1)}=D^{\mathsf T}\Delta_G^{(r)}\) when \(r\) is odd and \(\Delta_G^{(r+1)}=D\Delta_G^{(r)}\) when \(r\) is even. The order-\(k\) graph trend-filtering estimator is any solution of \[\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}}\frac12\|y-\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\Delta_G^{(k+1)}\beta\|_1.\] For \(k=0\), this reduces to graph total-variation denoising; higher \(k\) penalizes higher-order graph differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph trend filtering replaces ordered differences by recursively defined graph differences and applies an l1 penalty to the chosen higher-order difference vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Trend Filtering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The alternating incidence/transposed-incidence recursion is dimensionally consistent and the content kind fits the leaf, but graph trend-filtering conventions vary. A specific source is required to validate the recursion, order convention, and stated reduction at k=0.

children.title: Trend-Filtering Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Alternative parameterizations of trend-filtering structure.

children.title: Basis Representation
children.top_down_role: Trend-filtering structure expressed through basis coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract discrete-spline basis, independent of a particular falling-factorial normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=[N\ R]\). Then \(H\) is nonsingular, so every \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n\) has a unique representation \(\beta=H\theta=N\theta_{1:k+1}+R\theta_{k+2:n}\). Because \(DN=0\) and \(DR=I\), one has \(D\beta=\theta_{k+2:n}\). Consequently, for any convex loss \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(\lambda\ge0\), the basis-form problem is \[\min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^n} L(H\theta)+\lambda\|\theta_{k+2:n}\|_1.\] The first \(k+1\) coordinates parameterize the unpenalized null space, while the remaining coordinates equal the penalized differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A null-space basis completed by a right inverse converts the operator penalty into an l1 penalty on the non-null-space coefficients.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge k+2\), \(k\ge0\), and \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-k-1)\times n}\) has full row rank.
\(N\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(k+1)}\) is a basis matrix for \(\ker D\), and \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-k-1)}\) satisfies \(DR=I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta=H\theta\) and \(\|D\beta\|_1=\|\theta_{k+2:n}\|_1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: linear-algebraic null-space and right-inverse representation of an analysis penalty

children.title: Difference-Operator Representation
children.top_down_role: Trend-filtering structure expressed through penalized discrete differences.

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-Operator Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equally spaced discrete trend filtering with a forward-difference convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(D^{(0)}=I_n\) and \(D_m^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{(m-1)\times m}\) by \((D_m^{(1)}u)_i=u_{i+1}-u_i\). Set \(D^{(1)}=D_n^{(1)}\), and recursively define \(D^{(r+1)}=D_{n-r}^{(1)}D^{(r)}\) for \(r\ge1\). The order-\(k\) trend-filtering estimator is any solution of \[\widehat\beta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\frac12\|y-\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|D^{(k+1)}\beta\|_1\right\}.\] The penalty encourages \(D^{(k)}\widehat\beta\) to be piecewise constant in the discrete sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trend filtering minimizes squared error plus the l1 norm of the fitted sequence's order-(k+1) finite differences.
assumptions_latex: The observations are indexed on an equally spaced ordered grid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\beta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\frac12\|y-\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|D^{(k+1)}\beta\|_1\right\}.\)

notation.meaning: First forward-difference operator on vectors of length m.
Recursive difference operator of order r, with the zeroth-order operator equal to the identity.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard equally spaced trend-filtering analysis formulation

children.title: Parameterization Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between basis-domain and difference-domain descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterization Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence for any compatible null-space and right-inverse basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The maps \(\theta\mapsto\beta=H\theta\) and \(\beta\mapsto\theta=H^{-1}\beta\) are mutually inverse. Moreover, \(DH=[0\ I]\), so \[L(\beta)+\lambda\|D\beta\|_1=L(H\theta)+\lambda\|\theta_{k+2:n}\|_1.\] Thus objective values and minimizers correspond bijectively. In particular, \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{L(\beta)+\lambda\|D\beta\|_1\}=H\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{L(H\theta)+\lambda\|\theta_{k+2:n}\|_1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The invertible basis map gives the analysis and basis parameters identical objective values and corresponding minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge k+2\), \(k\ge0\), and \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-k-1)\times n}\) has full row rank.
\(N\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(k+1)}\) is a basis matrix for \(\ker D\), \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-k-1)}\) satisfies \(DR=I\), and \(H=[N\ R]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{L(\beta)+\lambda\|D\beta\|_1\}=H\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{L(H\theta)+\lambda\|\theta_{k+2:n}\|_1\}.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact invertible reparameterization of an operator l1 penalty

children.title: Boundary Effects
children.top_down_role: Endpoint and null-space behavior under alternative representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates harmless basis normalization from substantive finite-difference boundary conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed operator \(D\), every valid choice of \(N\) and \(R\) satisfying the assumptions gives an invertible coordinate map and represents the same objective \(L(\beta)+\lambda\|D\beta\|_1\). Hence the minimizer set in \(\beta\)-space is independent of the basis normalization. By contrast, replacing \(D\) with an operator \(\widetilde D\) having different endpoint rows defines the penalty \(\|\widetilde D\beta\|_1\), which may have a different null space and may produce a different minimizer set. A basis for the new convention must satisfy \(\widetilde D\widetilde H=[0\ I]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing coordinates for a fixed difference operator does not alter fitted minimizers, but changing endpoint differences can alter the penalty, its null space, and the boundary fit.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge k+2\), \(k\ge0\), and \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-k-1)\times n}\) has full row rank.
\(N\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(k+1)}\) is a basis matrix for \(\ker D\), \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-k-1)}\) satisfies \(DR=I\), and \(H=[N\ R]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta}\{L(\beta)+\lambda\|D\beta\|_1\}\) is invariant under valid basis changes for fixed \(D\), whereas replacing \(D\) by \(\widetilde D\) can change this minimizer set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: basis invariance and boundary dependence follow from the selected difference operator

children.title: Order-Shape Regularization Family
children.top_down_role: Soft structural penalties for ordering, monotonicity, and related shape information.

children.title: Nearly Isotonic Regularization
children.top_down_role: Soft enforcement of ordered monotonic structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\theta\in\arg\min_\theta \frac12\sum_i w_i(y_i-\theta_i)^2+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(\theta_i-\theta_{i+1})_+\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convex nearly isotonic least-squares formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondecreasing nearly isotonic regression with weighted squared loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The nondecreasing nearly isotonic estimator is any minimizer
\[\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(y_i-\theta_i)^2+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(\theta_i-\theta_{i+1})_+\right\}.\]
The penalty is convex, nonnegative, and equals zero exactly when \(\theta_1\le\cdots\le\theta_n\). Thus finite \(\lambda\) permits order violations at a linear cost rather than imposing monotonicity as a hard constraint. Reversing each difference gives the corresponding nonincreasing formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly isotonic regression penalizes, rather than forbids, adjacent violations of a specified monotone order.
